domain_assessment.domain: Elementary-school curriculum implementation and instructional improvement
domain_assessment.role: K-5 Curriculum Coordinator and instructional-coaching-cycle lead
domain_assessment.objective: Assess a trimester literacy-program pilot, prepare a defensible scale-up recommendation for the board and finance committee, and determine likely drivers of observed oral-reading-fluency outcomes.
domain_assessment.incident_type: Mid-pilot evidence evaluation and subsequent causal-attribution decision under budget competition and presentation deadlines.

decision_points.summary: The coordinator interprets mixed classroom-level oral-reading-fluency results and chooses to investigate testing conditions primarily in classrooms whose results do not align with expectations for Bridge Literacy.
evidence_before: Three classrooms were above expected growth and three were flat or mixed.
Testing occurred on different days across the two schools because of a scheduling conflict.
The coordinator had previously advocated for and introduced Bridge Literacy.
evidence_after: The literacy specialist reports that testing conditions were broadly similar across all six classrooms and that timing differences were not significant.
One flat classroom had unusually high absenteeism, a more plausible contributor to that classroom's result.
goals_constraints: Develop a reliable scale-up recommendation before the next budget cycle.
Present evidence that can withstand scrutiny amid competition for professional-development funding.
alternatives: Apply equivalent testing-condition scrutiny to all six classrooms.
Delay initial conclusions until the specialist audits all classrooms.
Treat the timing discrepancy as a general data-quality issue rather than a defect concentrated in disappointing results.
decision_points.decision_basis: The coordinator's attention was drawn selectively to classrooms where results did not match the expected program effect.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate; the board required a recommendation before the upcoming budget cycle.
decision_points.uncertainty: Moderate; the coordinator initially did not know whether testing-date variation, absenteeism, implementation differences, or the program itself explained between-classroom differences.

decision_points.summary: The coordinator chooses to present an aggregate trend-line highlights slide rather than six separate classroom profiles during a fifteen-minute board presentation.
evidence_before: The coordinator possessed the full six-classroom data set.
The coordinator and literacy specialist maintained a walkthrough-observation log.
The board agenda allowed fifteen minutes and the math intervention team was scheduled immediately afterward.
evidence_after: A board member requests classroom-by-classroom detail.
The coordinator can provide the data verbally but has not rehearsed presenting it in that format.
goals_constraints: Communicate results within a short agenda slot.
alternatives: Present all six classroom profiles on slides.
Provide an aggregate slide with a classroom-level appendix or handout.
Use a pre-briefed summary while making the complete disaggregated data visibly available.
decision_points.decision_basis: Presentation-time management rather than a stated desire to suppress unfavorable evidence.
decision_points.uncertainty: Low to moderate; the data existed, but the best presentation format under time constraints was uncertain.

decision_points.summary: The coordinator summarizes voluntary professional-development feedback while explicitly qualifying its representativeness and later flags possible differential nonresponse.
evidence_before: Five of six pilot teachers completed a voluntary survey and rated the coaching session helpful or very helpful.
One respondent stated that the pacing guide felt rushed for lower-performing students.
The initial survey sample was small and voluntary.
evidence_after: The specialist reports that two nonresponses involved invitations sent to teachers in flat-result classrooms.
The coordinator identifies this as a limitation rather than treating the responses as representative.
goals_constraints: Avoid overstating a small voluntary sample.
Maintain credibility in a politically consequential pilot recommendation.
alternatives: Treat the five positive responses as conclusive evidence of teacher support.
Contact nonrespondents immediately before summarizing results.
Report response counts, nonresponse uncertainty, and the critical pacing comment alongside favorable ratings.
decision_points.decision_basis: Explicit caveating of selection and nonresponse limitations.
decision_points.uncertainty: High; voluntary responses cannot establish the views of all pilot teachers.

decision_points.summary: The coordinator attributes modest aggregate fluency gains largely to the coaching cycle and recommends districtwide replication of the same coaching intensity, despite gains in two classrooms that did not receive the coordinator's direct coaching visits.
evidence_before: The aggregate result is a modest net gain across six classrooms.
The coordinator conducted biweekly coaching visits in four of the six classrooms.
The two non-visited classrooms also improved.
New decodable-text materials and smaller class sizes were present as possible co-occurring contributors.
evidence_after: A board member points out that improvement in non-visited classrooms complicates a coaching-centered explanation.
The coordinator acknowledges that further study is needed but continues to characterize coaching as the largest lever.
The coordinator says that, absent personal involvement, they would probably have examined materials and class-size differences more closely.
goals_constraints: Specify what resources would be required for scale-up.
Offer a plausible explanation for observed gains using imperfect observational pilot data.
alternatives: Describe coaching as one plausible contributor rather than the primary driver.
Withhold a primary-cause claim pending complete classroom-level data and a more systematic comparison.
Recommend a staged expansion that evaluates coaching, materials, class size, and attendance as competing or interacting explanations.
decision_points.decision_basis: The coordinator gives disproportionate causal weight to the intervention they personally implemented and observed directly.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate to high; the memo was drafted under deadline before all relevant classroom-level information was considered.
decision_points.uncertainty: High; the evidence is observational, multiple causes co-occurred, and the non-visited classrooms' improvement challenges a single-factor coaching explanation.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “Those looked like the program was doing what we hoped, so I didn't feel the same urgency to dig into how the testing was administered there.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision point 1; participant response immediately after the interviewer asks whether testing conditions in gain classrooms were examined comparably.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The coordinator evaluates the methodological adequacy of evidence asymmetrically: flat or mixed results prompt an active search for a testing-condition explanation, while favorable results are provisionally accepted without equivalent scrutiny. The asymmetry is tied to an antecedent favorable expectation for the program, shown by the participant's statement that the gain results were what was hoped for and the flat results did not match expectations.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: A legitimate triage rationale could be that anomalous or disappointing classrooms warrant investigation because they may signal implementation or measurement failures. However, the participant explicitly says the scheduling issue technically applied across the full testing window and that the asymmetry reflected attention to results that did not match expectations, which makes neutral anomaly triage insufficient as the complete explanation.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: No additional evidence is required for support. A more detailed contemporaneous statement of the coordinator's prior expectation would strengthen causal linkage between the favorable prior belief and the asymmetric evidence evaluation, but the current interview already provides that linkage.

revision.location: Decision point 1, in the exchange concerning whether testing conditions were examined in the classrooms showing gains.
revision.current_defect: No occurrence-level defect. The later reflective statements make the mechanism somewhat more visible than a highly subtle naturalistic instance, but they do not create a second distinct occurrence.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the current exchange. Do not add another separate episode in which favorable and unfavorable pilot results receive unequal methodological scrutiny.
preserve: The mixed six-classroom fluency result pattern.
The testing-schedule discrepancy as a plausible initial explanation.
The coordinator's differential scrutiny of flat versus gain classrooms.
The later specialist finding that the timing difference was not significant.
avoid_creating: A second confirmation-oriented or biased-assimilation episode at the board-presentation or survey-feedback decision points.
An explicit textbook-style bias label in the participant's speech.
A stronger claim that the coordinator deliberately manipulated data.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “When I wrote the memo, I framed the gains as largely a product of that coaching cycle” and “I'd probably have looked harder at the materials and class-size differences if I weren't the one who ran the coaching.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision point 4; recommendation-memo discussion, especially the response to the hypothetical involving another person's identical result.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The coordinator overattributes a shared, multi-factor outcome to their own coaching contribution. They give central causal weight to the work they personally performed, discount improvement in two classrooms without direct coaching, and acknowledge that the causal weighting would likely change if another person had run the coaching. This self-referential asymmetry supports egocentric attribution rather than merely an informed judgment about a familiar intervention.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The coordinator had direct observation of the coaching process and may reasonably view it as an important contributor. The evidence nevertheless does not establish coaching as the primary cause, because gains also occurred in non-visited classrooms and materials, class-size, attendance, and other implementation conditions were not systematically separated. The participant's self-other counterfactual further supports an egocentric mechanism.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: No additional evidence is needed to establish the occurrence. A local chronology clarification is needed because the interview first states that the coordinator had the full six-classroom data set for board preparation, then says they did not see non-visited classroom data until after submitting the memo.

revision.location: Decision point 4, the answer beginning “Probably if I'd seen the non-visited classrooms' data before drafting, instead of after submitting it.”
revision.current_defect: The stated timing of the non-visited classroom data is potentially inconsistent with the prior board-preparation account that the coordinator had the full six-classroom data set. This ambiguity can make the overattribution appear to arise from missing information rather than selective self-attribution.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Clarify that the coordinator had the aggregate result and preliminary classroom outcomes when preparing the board materials, but did not receive or integrate the complete disaggregated non-visited-classroom comparison, including the relevant implementation-context details, before drafting the causal section of the recommendation memo. Preserve the coordinator's continued claim that coaching was the main lever and the later admission that another person's coaching would have led them to inspect materials and class size more closely.
preserve: The four coached and two non-visited classroom arrangement.
Observed gains in the two non-visited classrooms.
The presence of decodable-text materials and smaller class sizes as alternative contributors.
The coordinator's recommendation for districtwide coaching capacity.
The self-other counterfactual cue supporting egocentric attribution.
avoid_creating: A second causal-attribution episode in which the coordinator independently repeats the same coaching-centered conclusion.
A claim that coaching definitively caused gains.
A new bias at decision point 2 based on selective omission of classroom-level data from the board slide.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “Those looked like the program was doing what we hoped, so I didn't feel the same urgency to dig into how the testing was administered there.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The participant privileges evidence consistent with a favorable expectation and directs scrutiny toward inconsistent evidence.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: This is not an independent additional occurrence. It is the same evidence trace and the same asymmetric-evidence-evaluation mechanism already more specifically captured as Biased Assimilation. Double-labeling it as a separate confirmation-bias occurrence would inflate the count.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “I'd probably have looked harder at the materials and class-size differences if I weren't the one who ran the coaching.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The participant's own contribution receives elevated causal weight in an outcome that could reflect multiple contributors.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The transcript supports egocentric overattribution, but it does not separately establish a self-esteem-protective motive, credit-claiming motive, or a comparison between personal credit for success and externalization of blame for failure. Treating self-serving bias as an additional occurrence would duplicate the intended egocentric-bias episode.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “The coaching piece was what I had the most direct visibility into.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: Directly observed coaching activity may be more cognitively available and therefore receive disproportionate causal weight relative to less visible contextual factors.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Direct visibility is also a legitimate reason to speak more confidently about coaching than about factors the coordinator had not observed. The self-other counterfactual makes egocentric bias the better account, but the present wording alone does not establish a separate availability-based occurrence.

nonbias_cues.cue: The coordinator uses an aggregate highlights slide rather than displaying all six classroom profiles during a fifteen-minute board slot.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The participant gives a concrete operational reason—limited presentation time—and retains the complete data for questions. A board member requests detail and receives it. The account does not show selective concealment, motivated omission, or a distorted inference from the aggregate display.

nonbias_cues.cue: The coordinator does not immediately follow up with a teacher who did not complete the voluntary professional-development survey.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Delayed follow-up alone is an ordinary process limitation. More importantly, once potential differential nonresponse is identified, the coordinator treats it as a limitation and does not generalize the favorable responses to all teachers.

nonbias_cues.cue: The coordinator notes that five of six survey respondents rated the coaching session helpful or very helpful.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The participant explicitly identifies the voluntary, small-sample caveat and avoids presenting the result as definitive evidence of general teacher sentiment. This is calibrated uncertainty rather than biased generalization.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant says that a flat classroom's unusually high absenteeism probably mattered more than testing timing.
nonbias_cues.location: Decision point 1; after the specialist's follow-up.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: This is a plausible contextual explanation offered after testing-condition similarity is checked. The transcript does not show the coordinator using absenteeism selectively to protect a favored conclusion after it is known; it is reported as a newly available explanatory factor.

nonbias_cues.cue: The board member challenges the coaching-centered explanation and the coordinator acknowledges that more study is needed.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Disagreement, uncertainty, and a provisional response are not biases by themselves. The egocentric-bias inference rests instead on the coordinator's self-referential causal weighting and their stated self-other difference in how they would evaluate alternatives.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant retrospectively recognizes that testing conditions should have been reviewed across all classrooms before forming an impression.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: This is metacognitive correction and procedural learning. It describes the earlier biased-assimilation occurrence but is not a new, independent instance of biased processing.

causal_claims.claim: The observed aggregate fluency gain was largely a product of the coordinator's biweekly coaching cycle.
evidence_offered: Biweekly coaching visits occurred in four of six classrooms.
The coordinator observed coaching activities and perceived them as influential week to week.
key_unaddressed_alternatives: Improvement in two classrooms without the coordinator's direct coaching visits.
Potential baseline differences, teacher effects, instructional fidelity, and regression or ordinary variation.
causal_claims.assessment: Causally underidentified. The observational pilot provides temporal association and implementation exposure, but it does not isolate coaching's incremental effect or justify a primary-cause conclusion.

causal_claims.claim: Testing-day timing could explain flat classroom results.
causal_claims.claim_location: Decision point 1; initial response to mixed results.
evidence_offered: Testing occurred on different days because of a scheduling conflict.
key_unaddressed_alternatives: Whether the schedule difference applied equally across classrooms.
Actual similarity of testing administration conditions.
causal_claims.assessment: Appropriately treated as a hypothesis at first, but the participant's selective attention to it in flat classrooms rather than across the full sample creates an evidence-evaluation problem. The specialist's later finding weakens the timing explanation.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Coaching intensity is confounded with the coordinator's own involvement, possible classroom selection, teacher differences, and co-occurring resources.
correlation_causation_risks.implication: The memo should not treat observed gains as evidence that coaching was the largest causal lever without a comparison strategy or stronger implementation and baseline data.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Aggregate gains mask heterogeneous classroom-level outcomes and may obscure whether similar gains arose through different mechanisms.
correlation_causation_risks.implication: A scale-up recommendation can reasonably identify coaching as a resource requirement or hypothesis, but not as an established primary cause.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: The initial concern about testing timing was applied after observing outcome direction and not assessed symmetrically.
correlation_causation_risks.implication: Data-quality checks should be pre-specified or applied across all classrooms before causal or program-effect interpretations are made.

causal_audit.changed_variable: The interview contains two diagnostic hypotheticals: the identity of the person who conducted coaching, and the timing of access to complete non-visited-classroom data. These are probes of the participant's attribution process, not a formal paired-scenario counterfactual manipulation.
held_constant: The reported pilot outcomes in the hypothetical involving another person's coaching are intended to remain the same.
The occupational setting and available alternative causal factors remain broadly constant.
causal_audit.explanation: The self-other hypothetical is diagnostically useful because it holds the result broadly constant while varying the participant's personal involvement; the participant says their causal weighting would change. However, the interview's chronology needs clarification because the participant is said to have the full six-classroom data set before the board meeting but later says they did not see non-visited classroom data before drafting the memo. The scenario is not designated as a paired counterfactual condition, so no formal counterfactual-fidelity requirement is violated.

global_revision_constraints: Preserve exactly four decision points: mixed-result evaluation, board-data presentation, professional-development survey interpretation, and recommendation-memo causal attribution.
Preserve exactly one distinct Biased Assimilation occurrence at decision point 1 and exactly one distinct Egocentric bias occurrence at decision point 4.
Do not convert the participant's reflective admissions into textbook labels or overt declarations of bias.
Do not treat the aggregation choice at decision point 2 or the survey caveating at decision point 3 as additional bias occurrences.
Clarify information timing without removing the independent evidence that the participant overweights personally delivered coaching.
Do not introduce a new causal variable or alter the scenario's occupational setting, role, timeline, or budget-pressure context.

revision_order.action: Clarify the timing and granularity of classroom-level data available before the causal recommendation memo, so the causal attribution remains distinguishable from an ordinary decision made under genuinely missing information.
No substantive revision required; retain the existing asymmetric-scrutiny exchange without adding duplicate instances.

failure_flags.location: Transition between board-meeting preparation and recommendation-memo discussion.
failure_flags.description: The participant reports having the full six-classroom data set for board preparation, then says they would have weighted alternatives differently if they had seen non-visited-classroom data before drafting the memo. The text should distinguish preliminary/aggregate data from later-received or later-integrated disaggregated comparison data.

failure_flags.location: Decision point 4 and subsequent follow-up probes.
failure_flags.description: The coaching-centered causal claim is revisited in several adjacent answers. These should be treated as one continuous evidence trace rather than multiple occurrences, but the repeated probing slightly reduces the hidden-label subtlety and should not be expanded further.
